title: Into Madinah
subtitle: A Friday prayer in a valley, a camel left to choose, a mosque of mud brick, and a city that had to become home

units.title: The first Friday, in Wādī Rānūnāʾ

when.label: A Friday in Rabīʿ al-Awwal, year 1 of the Hijra (622 CE)

place.note: The present-day Masjid al-Jumuʿa is identified with the spot by tradition; the point is approximate.

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq says that God brought the Prophet ﷺ out from among Banū ʿAmr b. ʿAwf at Qubāʾ on a Friday.
He adds that Banū ʿAmr b. ʿAwf claimed the Prophet ﷺ stayed with them longer than Ibn Isḥāq's count, and closes the matter with 'God knows best which it was'.
statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq himself records that the clan of Qubāʾ gave a longer stay than his own account; he does not decide between them.

statements.text: The time of the Friday prayer came upon him among Banū Sālim b. ʿAwf, and he prayed it in the mosque in the bed of the valley, Wādī Rānūnāʾ.
Ibn Isḥāq counts this as the first Friday prayer the Prophet ﷺ led in Madinah.
Between the present-day mosque of Qubāʾ and the present-day Masjid al-Jumuʿa the straight-line distance is about 2.3 km, to the north-west.
statements.basis: computed distance and bearing between gazetteer points (both approximate)

statements.text: Rānūnāʾ is a wadi bed: low ground where seasonal water runs between the date gardens of the southern oasis.
statements.basis: terrain data; the name 'bed of the valley' in the source

people.name: Banū Sālim b. ʿAwf
people.who: A clan of the Khazraj living between Qubāʾ and the heart of the oasis
people.here: The first Friday prayer in Madinah was held in their valley

reveal.text: The day's ride from Qubāʾ to the Friday prayer was short: on today's map the two mosques lie about 2.3 km apart.

question.q: Where did the Prophet ﷺ lead his first Friday prayer in Madinah, according to Ibn Isḥāq?

options.text: Among Banū Sālim b. ʿAwf, in the bed of Wādī Rānūnāʾ
options.why: Ibn Isḥāq names the clan and the valley.

options.text: At the site where the camel later knelt
options.why: The camel had not yet knelt; that came after the Friday prayer, further into the oasis.

options.text: In Qubāʾ, before leaving
options.why: He had left Qubāʾ that Friday; the prayer caught up with him on the way.

units.matters: Reflection: the first communal Friday in the new home was held on the road, in a clan's valley, not in a finished mosque. Worship came before the building.

units.title: “Let her go, she is under command”
units.kicker: Clan after clan takes the camel's rein

when.label: The same Friday, after the prayer

statements.text: ʿItbān b. Mālik and ʿAbbās b. ʿUbāda b. Naḍla came with men of Banū Sālim and asked the Prophet ﷺ to stay with them, offering their numbers, their arms and their protection.
He answered, speaking of his she-camel, 'Let her go her way, for she is under command', and they let her go.

The same invitation and the same answer are repeated at the dwellings of Banū Bayāḍa (Ziyād b. Labīd and Farwa b. ʿAmr), of Banū Sāʿida (Saʿd b. ʿUbāda and al-Mundhir b. ʿAmr) and of Banū al-Ḥārith b. al-Khazraj (Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ, Khārija b. Zayd and ʿAbd Allāh b. Rawāḥa).
At Banū ʿAdī b. al-Najjār, Salīṭ b. Qays and Abū Salīṭ called him to 'your maternal uncles', because Salmā bint ʿAmr, the mother of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, was one of their women.
Five clans, five offers of protection, and the same reply each time: the source gives no clan the choice.
Madinah was not one town but a spread of clan settlements, gardens and fortified houses across a basin ringed by lava fields.
statements.basis: terrain data; settlement pattern implied by the clan dwellings the source lists

people.name: ʿItbān b. Mālik
people.here: First to ask him to stay

people.name: Saʿd b. ʿUbāda
people.who: Chief of Banū Sāʿida, a naqīb at the ʿAqaba pledge
people.here: Stopped the camel at his clan's dwellings

reveal.text: From Masjid al-Jumuʿa to the site where the camel knelt is about 2 km in a straight line, to the north-north-east; the clan dwellings lay somewhere along that way, and their exact spots are not fixed.
reveal.basis: computed distance between gazetteer points; the dwellings are unlocated

question.q: Every clan offers numbers, weapons and protection. What do you expect him to say at the next one?

options.text: The same: 'Let her go, she is under command'
options.why: Ibn Isḥāq repeats the identical reply at every clan.

options.text: He accepts the clan of his maternal kin
options.why: Even Banū ʿAdī b. al-Najjār, who appealed to kinship, received the same reply.

units.matters: Reflection: leaving the choice to the camel meant no clan could claim to have won him over another. A city of rival clans received a guest none of them had chosen.

units.title: The drying-ground of two orphans
units.kicker: The camel kneels at Banū Mālik b. al-Najjār

place.note: The present-day mosque stands on the site.

lights.name: Sahl and Suhayl, the two orphans

statements.text: At the dwellings of Banū Mālik b. al-Najjār the camel knelt at what became the door of the Prophet's mosque ﷺ. It was then a mirbad, a place for drying dates, belonging to two orphan boys, Sahl and Suhayl, sons of ʿAmr.

Ibn Isḥāq describes the camel kneeling, rising and going a little way while the Prophet ﷺ left her rein slack, then turning back to the first spot, kneeling again and settling her neck on the ground. Only then did he dismount.
Abū Ayyūb Khālid b. Zayd carried the saddle into his house, and the Prophet ﷺ lodged with him.
Asked who owned the drying-ground, Muʿādh b. ʿAfrāʾ said it belonged to Sahl and Suhayl, orphans in his care, and that he would satisfy them for it; and it was taken as a mosque.
In al-Bukhārī's version the orphans were in the care of Asʿad b. Zurāra; the Prophet ﷺ bargained with them, they offered it as a gift, and he declined and bought it.
statements.note: The sources differ on the guardian (Muʿādh b. ʿAfrāʾ in Ibn Isḥāq, Asʿad b. Zurāra in al-Bukhārī) and on how the price was settled; in Anas's report (al-Bukhārī 428) Banū al-Najjār say they seek its price only from God.

statements.text: Anas reports that the plot held graves of polytheists, ruins and palm trees; the graves were dug up, the ruins levelled, and the palms cut down.

people.name: Sahl and Suhayl b. ʿAmr
people.who: Two orphan boys of Banū Mālik b. al-Najjār

people.name: Muʿādh b. ʿAfrāʾ
people.who: Their guardian in Ibn Isḥāq's account
people.here: Promised to satisfy them for the land

people.name: Abū Ayyūb Khālid b. Zayd
people.here: Took the saddle into his house

reveal.text: The site of the camel's kneeling now lies within the Prophet's Mosque; the exact boundaries of the first plot are not marked on this map.
reveal.basis: gazetteer point for the present-day mosque

question.q: Who owned the ground where the camel knelt?

options.text: Two orphan boys, Sahl and Suhayl
options.why: Both Ibn Isḥāq and al-Bukhārī name the two orphans.

options.text: Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī
options.why: Abū Ayyūb hosted him; the land belonged to the orphans.

options.text: Saʿd b. ʿUbāda
options.why: Saʿd stopped the camel at Banū Sāʿida, earlier on the way.

units.matters: Reflection: the centre of the new community was a date-drying yard of two orphans, paid for rather than simply taken.

units.title: Downstairs at Abū Ayyūb's
units.kicker: A guest in a two-storey house

when.label: From Rabīʿ al-Awwal, year 1, until the houses were built

place.note: Abū Ayyūb's house was near the mosque site; its exact spot is not fixed here.

statements.text: Abū Ayyūb, through a chain Ibn Isḥāq names, says the Prophet ﷺ took the lower floor while he and Umm Ayyūb lived above.
Abū Ayyūb said he hated to be above him and asked him to move up; the Prophet ﷺ answered that the lower floor was easier for them and for those who came to see him.
When a water jar broke upstairs, Abū Ayyūb and Umm Ayyūb mopped the water with the only blanket they had, for fear a drop would fall on him below.
They sent his supper down, and when food came back they ate from where his hand had been, seeking blessing.
One night a dish with onion or garlic came back untouched. He explained that he found its smell, and he was a man who spoke in private with the angel, but told them to eat it.

He stayed in Abū Ayyūb's house until his mosque and dwellings were built, then moved into them. Ibn Isḥāq puts that stay in Madinah before the houses were ready from Rabīʿ al-Awwal into Ṣafar of the following year.

people.name: Abū Ayyūb Khālid b. Zayd
people.here: Host for many months; narrator of this account

people.name: Umm Ayyūb
people.here: Shared the care of the guest below

reveal.text: The chain runs Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, from Marthad b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazanī, from Abū Ruhm al-Samāʿī, from Abū Ayyūb himself.

units.matters: Reflection: the guest chose the floor that was easier for visitors; the hosts gave their only blanket. Hospitality is told here in small, domestic things.

units.title: Building with their own hands
units.kicker: The mosque and the houses rise

statements.text: The Prophet ﷺ ordered the mosque built and worked on it himself, to make the Muslims keen to work; Muhājirūn and Anṣār laboured at it steadily.
One of the Muslims said in verse that if they sat while the Prophet ﷺ worked, theirs would be a misguided deed.

As they built they chanted: 'There is no life but the life of the Hereafter; O God, have mercy on the Anṣār and the Muhājira.' Ibn Isḥāq says the Prophet ﷺ answered with the same words, naming the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār.
Ibn Hishām remarks that this line is speech, not true rajaz metre.
In Anas's report the cut palm trunks were set in a row toward the qibla, with stone for the door-jambs, and the Prophet ﷺ chanted with them as they carried stones.

Ibn Hishām adds a rajaz couplet that ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib is said to have chanted, on those who build mosques and those who shy from the dust, but scholars of poetry he asked could not say whether ʿAlī composed it.
statements.note: Ibn Hishām's informants said only that it reached them as ʿAlī's chant; authorship is uncertain.

reveal.text: Jabal Uḥud stands about 4.8 km almost due north of the mosque site, the largest landmark on the oasis skyline.
reveal.basis: computed distance and bearing between gazetteer points

question.q: Why, according to Ibn Isḥāq, did the Prophet ﷺ work on the building himself?

options.text: To make the Muslims keen to work on it
options.why: Ibn Isḥāq gives exactly this reason.

options.text: Because there were not enough workers
options.why: The source says Muhājirūn and Anṣār laboured steadily; it gives a different reason.

units.matters: Reflection: the first shared project of the two groups was a building of mud and palm trunks, with the leader carrying loads alongside them.

units.title: ʿAmmār and the bricks

statements.text: ʿAmmār b. Yāsir came in loaded with mud bricks and said, 'They are killing me; they load on me what they do not carry themselves.'

Umm Salama said she saw the Prophet ﷺ shake out ʿAmmār's curly hair with his hand, saying, 'Woe, son of Sumayya! They are not the ones who will kill you; the rebel party (al-fiʾa al-bāghiya) will kill you.'
The words 'the rebel party will kill ʿAmmār' are transmitted in the ṣaḥīḥ collections, from Umm Salama in Muslim and from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī in al-Bukhārī's chapter on building the mosque.
Ibn Isḥāq reports that ʿAmmār took up the building chant; a Companion thought he was aiming it at him and threatened him with a stick. Ibn Isḥāq named the man, but Ibn Hishām left the name out.
The Prophet ﷺ grew angry and said that ʿAmmār called them to Paradise while they called him to the Fire, and that ʿAmmār was to him like the skin between his eyes and nose.
Ibn Hishām cites al-Shaʿbī that the first person to build a mosque was ʿAmmār b. Yāsir.
statements.note: A single opinion of al-Shaʿbī transmitted by Ibn Hishām outside Ibn Isḥāq's text; other reports credit the mosque at Qubāʾ or earlier prayer places, so 'first' is contested.

people.name: ʿAmmār b. Yāsir
people.who: Early Muslim, son of Sumayya, ally of Banū Makhzūm
people.here: Carried bricks; the subject of the saying

people.name: Umm Salama
people.here: Narrator of the scene in Ibn Isḥāq

reveal.text: ʿAmmār was later killed at Ṣiffīn (37 AH), fighting on ʿAlī's side, and the saying became central to how the Muslims judged that conflict.

sources.ref: Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kabīr, biography of ʿAmmār b. Yāsir
sources.note: Death at Ṣiffīn and the citing of the saying there

sources.ref: al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk, events of the year 37

question.q: In Umm Salama's account, what did the Prophet ﷺ say about who would kill ʿAmmār?

options.text: Not those loading the bricks, but the rebel party
options.why: This is the wording Ibn Isḥāq gives from Umm Salama, and the core is in Muslim.

options.text: That nobody would harm him
options.why: The saying speaks of his being killed by the rebel party.

units.matters: Reflection: a joke about heavy bricks on a building site became a saying that later generations read in the light of civil war.

units.title: Locked houses in Makkah
units.kicker: The emigrants catch up; what they left behind

when.label: Year 1 of the Hijra and after

statements.text: The emigrants followed the Prophet ﷺ until none remained in Makkah except someone seduced from the faith or held captive.

Ibn Isḥāq names the households that left with all their families and property: Banū Maẓʿūn of Jumaḥ, Banū Jaḥsh b. Riʾāb, allies of Banū Umayya, and Banū al-Bukayr, allies of Banū ʿAdī. Their houses in Makkah were locked, with no one living in them.
Abū Sufyān b. Ḥarb seized the empty house of Banū Jaḥsh and sold it to ʿAmr b. ʿAlqama of Banū ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy.
When ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh told the Prophet ﷺ, he asked whether he would not be content for God to give him a better house in Paradise; ʿAbd Allāh said yes, and was told 'that is yours'.

After the conquest of Makkah, Abū Aḥmad raised the house again. People told him the Prophet ﷺ disliked that they take back property lost for God's sake, and he stopped; he addressed a poem of reproach to Abū Sufyān instead.

quran.gist: A share of what God grants is for the poor emigrants who were driven from their homes and property, seeking God's favour and supporting God and His Messenger; they are the truthful.
quran.context: The verse speaks of emigrants expelled from homes and goods, which is the situation Ibn Isḥāq describes for the locked houses; the link is thematic, made here, not stated in the source for this episode.

people.name: ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh
people.who: Emigrant, of a family allied to Banū Umayya
people.here: Lost his family house to Abū Sufyān

people.name: Abū Aḥmad b. Jaḥsh
people.here: Raised the matter after the conquest

reveal.text: Makkah lies about 340 km south of Madinah in a straight line.

question.q: Years later, Makkah is conquered. Will the Prophet ﷺ restore the Jaḥsh house to its family?

options.text: No; he disliked their taking back what they had lost for God
options.why: People told Abū Aḥmad so, and he stopped asking.

options.text: Yes, it is returned at once
options.why: Ibn Isḥāq says the Prophet ﷺ was slow to answer and the family let it go.

units.matters: Reflection: the Hijra had a price that stayed paid, even after victory made it possible to reclaim it.

units.title: The first sermon

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq gives the first sermon of the Prophet ﷺ only as 'what reached me from Abū Salama b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān', adding 'we seek refuge with God from saying of him what he did not say'.
statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq's own hedge: it reached him (balaghanī) from a Successor, with no connected chain to the Prophet ﷺ.

statements.text: In it, after praising God, he tells the people to send ahead good for themselves: each will be struck down and leave his flock without a shepherd, and his Lord will ask him, with no interpreter and no veil between them, what he sent ahead.
statements.note: Same hedged report from Abū Salama.

statements.text: The sermon ends: whoever can shield his face from the Fire even with half a date should do so, and whoever cannot, with a good word, for a good deed is repaid tenfold up to seven hundredfold.
statements.note: The setting as the 'first sermon' rests on the hedged report; the core teaching itself is authenticated separately (next statement).

statements.text: The teaching 'guard yourselves from the Fire even with half a date, and if you find nothing, then with a good word' is transmitted in al-Bukhārī from ʿAdī b. Ḥātim.

sources.ref: al-Bukhārī, Kitāb al-Zakāt, bāb ittaqū al-nār wa-law bi-shiqq tamra (and Kitāb al-Riqāq)

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq then gives a second sermon: the best speech is the Book of God; love what God loves; love God with all your hearts; do not tire of God's words; and love one another by the spirit of God.

reveal.text: Ibn Isḥāq inserts a protective formula inside the very sentence that introduces the sermon, signalling that he is passing on a report, not vouching for its wording.

question.q: How sure is Ibn Isḥāq about the wording of the first sermon?

options.text: Not sure: it 'reached him' from Abū Salama, and he adds a prayer against misquoting the Prophet ﷺ
options.why: Both the hedge and the formula are in his text.

options.text: Certain: he gives an eyewitness chain
options.why: No eyewitness chain is given for this sermon.

units.matters: Reflection: whatever its exact wording, the first message remembered for the new city was about the Day of Judgment and small charity, not about power.

units.title: A written compact for Yathrib

when.label: Early Madinan period; exact date debated

lights.name: the believers of Quraysh and Yathrib

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq says the Prophet ﷺ wrote a document between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār in which he made a pact with the Jews, confirming them in their religion and property, with conditions on both sides.
The document calls the believers of Quraysh and Yathrib, and those who joined them and strove with them, 'one community (umma) apart from other people'.

Each group, the Muhājirūn and each Anṣārī clan by name, keeps its customary way of paying blood-money and ransoming its captives, 'with fairness among the believers'; and the believers are not to leave a debt-burdened man unhelped.
It states that the Jews of Banū ʿAwf are a community with the believers, 'to the Jews their religion and to the Muslims theirs', and extends the same to the Jews of the other named clans.
It declares the interior of Yathrib sacred for the people of the document, and refers any dispute among them to God and to Muḥammad ﷺ.
Ibn Isḥāq gives the text without a chain, and scholars differ on whether it is one document or several joined together, and on when it was written.
statements.note: No isnād in Ibn Isḥāq; its unity and date (before or after Badr) are debated in classical and modern scholarship.

discover.label: See the oasis as one place

reveal.text: From high above, Qubāʾ in the south and Uḥud in the north fall inside one view of roughly 8 km: the space the compact tried to make a single protected interior.

units.matters: Reflection: alongside the mosque, a written agreement: the new community was organised by worship and by law at the same time.

units.title: Brothers in pairs
units.kicker: The muʾākhāt between Muhājirūn and Anṣār

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq says the Prophet ﷺ made his Companions from the Muhājirūn and Anṣār brothers, and reports with the hedge 'as it reached us' that he said 'Be brothers in God, two by two', then took ʿAlī's hand and said 'This is my brother'.
statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq hedges the wording ('fīmā balaghanā') and adds a formula against misquoting.

statements.text: His list pairs, among others, Abū Bakr with Khārija b. Zuhayr, ʿUmar with ʿItbān b. Mālik, Abū ʿUbayda with Saʿd b. Muʿādh, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf with Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ, Muṣʿab b. ʿUmayr with Abū Ayyūb, and Salmān al-Fārisī with Abū al-Dardāʾ.

Some pairings come with alternatives ('it is said'): al-Zubayr with Salāma b. Salāma or with ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd; ʿAmmār with Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān or with Thābit b. Qays. Ibn Hishām notes that Jaʿfar, listed with Muʿādh b. Jabal, was then in Abyssinia.
statements.note: The list itself records variant pairings, and Ibn Hishām flags Jaʿfar's absence.

statements.text: Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ offered ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf half his wealth; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān asked instead to be shown the market, and traded.
Ibn ʿAbbās reports that at first a Muhājir inherited from his Anṣārī brother rather than from kin, until a verse of al-Nisāʾ (4:33) ended this.
Years later, when ʿUmar organised the army registers in Syria, Bilāl asked to be registered with Abū Ruwayḥa, 'I will never leave him', because of the brotherhood the Prophet ﷺ had made between them.

quran.gist: Those who believed, emigrated and strove, and those who gave them shelter and help, are allies of one another.
quran.context: The verse names the two groups the brotherhood joined; the link is thematic. Grade of the verse itself: established.

people.name: Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ
people.here: Offered his brother half his wealth

people.name: Abū Ruwayḥa ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Khathʿamī
people.here: Bilāl's register was joined to his

discover.label: A brotherhood that outlived the founders

reveal.text: Ibn Isḥāq says that, because of Bilāl's choice, the register of the Abyssinians was joined to Khathʿam in Syria, and remained so 'to this day'.

question.q: What did ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf ask of Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ?

options.text: To be shown the market
options.why: He declined the half share and asked for the market.

options.text: Half of his wealth
options.why: That was Saʿd's offer, which ʿAbd al-Raḥmān declined.

units.matters: Reflection: refugees and hosts were bound person to person, not only group to group; and the bond was remembered a generation later in a distant army.

units.title: The death of Asʿad b. Zurāra
units.kicker: The first naqīb is lost while the mosque is still rising

statements.text: Abū Umāma Asʿad b. Zurāra died in those months while the mosque was being built, taken by an illness of the throat (dhubḥa) or of the breath (shahqa).

Through a descendant of Asʿad, Ibn Isḥāq reports that the Prophet ﷺ called it a grievous death, because the Jews and the hypocrites among the Arabs would say 'had he been a prophet, his companion would not have died'.
In the same report the Prophet ﷺ adds that he has no power, for himself or for his companion, over anything from God.
Asʿad had been the naqīb of Banū al-Najjār. They came asking the Prophet ﷺ to appoint one of them in his place.
He answered: 'You are my maternal uncles; I am with you in what you have, and I am your naqīb', disliking to favour some of them over others.
Ibn Isḥāq notes that Banū al-Najjār counted it among their honours over their people that the Prophet ﷺ was their naqīb.

people.name: Abū Umāma Asʿad b. Zurāra
people.who: Of Banū al-Najjār; among the first of Yathrib to accept Islam, a naqīb at the second ʿAqaba
people.here: Died while the mosque was being built

reveal.text: The saying about his death comes through ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Bakr, from Yaḥyā b. ʿAbd Allāh, a great-grandson of Asʿad; the naqīb episode comes through ʿĀṣim b. ʿUmar b. Qatāda.

question.q: Banū al-Najjār ask for a new naqīb from among themselves. What will he do?

options.text: Take the role himself, so no one of them is preferred
options.why: He named himself their naqīb, disliking to single out some over others.

options.text: Appoint Abū Ayyūb, his host
options.why: No such appointment is reported; he took the role himself.

units.matters: Reflection: the new community's first loss was also a test of its claims, and the answer given was that a prophet does not control death.

units.title: The fever of Madinah

statements.text: ʿĀʾisha said that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah it was the most fever-ridden land of God, and his Companions suffered illness from it, while God spared him.

Abū Bakr, ʿĀmir b. Fuhayra and Bilāl shared one house and all fell ill. ʿĀʾisha, visiting before the veil was imposed, asked her father how he felt; he answered with a verse: every man wakes among his family, and death is nearer than his sandal-strap.
ʿĀmir b. Fuhayra answered her with verses about tasting death before it came. ʿĀʾisha said neither man knew what he was saying.

When the fever left Bilāl he lay in the courtyard and sang of whether he would ever again spend a night at Fakhkh among idhkhir grass, drink at the waters of Majanna, or see Shāma and Ṭafīl, which Ibn Hishām explains are two mountains of Makkah.

ʿĀʾisha told the Prophet ﷺ, and he prayed: 'O God, make Madinah beloved to us as You made Makkah beloved, or more; bless us in its mudd and its ṣāʿ; and move its fever to Mahyaʿa', which Ibn Hishām says is al-Juḥfa.

Ibn Isḥāq also reports, from al-Zuhrī via ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr, that the sick Companions prayed sitting; the Prophet ﷺ told them a seated prayer earns half of a standing one, and they forced themselves to stand despite their weakness.

people.name: ʿĀmir b. Fuhayra
people.who: Freedman of Abū Bakr who tended the flock near Thawr
people.here: Fell ill in the same house

people.name: Bilāl
people.who: Freedman of Abū Bakr, later the muezzin
people.here: Sang of Makkah's places in his fever

reveal.text: Al-Juḥfa, identified by Ibn Hishām with Mahyaʿa, lies about 214 km south-south-west of Madinah toward the coast.
Fakhkh, Majanna, Shāma and Ṭafīl are named places in and around Makkah; their positions are not fixed on this map.

question.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ ask for Madinah when he heard of the fever?

options.text: That it be made as beloved as Makkah, or more, blessed in its measures, and its fever moved to al-Juḥfa
options.why: This is the prayer ʿĀʾisha reports.

options.text: That the Companions return to Makkah
options.why: The prayer is for Madinah to become beloved, not for a return.

units.matters: Reflection: the sources keep the homesickness of the emigrants in plain view, and the remedy asked for was love for the new place, not forgetting the old.

units.title: “The full moon has risen over us”
units.kicker: A famous welcome song, and what the sources can bear

when.label: Arrival in Madinah, year 1 (or, on another view, the return from Tabūk, year 9)

place.note: A pass on the edge of Madinah; which side of the city it lay on is part of the debate.

statements.text: Al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib said he never saw the people of Madinah rejoice at anything as they rejoiced at the coming of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to the point that young servant girls were saying 'The Messenger of Allah has come'.

The song beginning 'ṭalaʿa al-badru ʿalaynā, min thaniyyāt al-wadāʿ' ('the full moon has risen over us from the passes of farewell') is not in Ibn Isḥāq's account of the arrival, nor in the ṣaḥīḥ collections.

sources.ref: al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa, chapter on the arrival in Madinah

statements.note: Absence from Ibn Isḥāq and the ṣaḥīḥ works is noted; the song is known from later compilations.

statements.text: Its best-known source is a report in al-Bayhaqī's Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa through Ibn ʿĀʾisha, a third-century scholar, without a connected chain back to the event; Ibn Ḥajar describes the chain as broken (muʿḍal).

sources.note: Comment on the chain of the welcome song

statements.note: Weak, disconnected chain; the attribution to the Hijra arrival cannot be confirmed.

statements.text: Ibn al-Qayyim argued that the song belongs to the return from Tabūk, because the Thaniyyat al-Wadāʿ pass lay on the Syria side of Madinah, not on the road from Makkah; others kept it at the Hijra.
statements.note: Scholars differ on the occasion: arrival in year 1 versus return from Tabūk in year 9.

statements.text: Qubāʾ and the road from Makkah approach Madinah from the south, while Uḥud and the routes to Syria lie to the north.

reveal.text: From the north, looking south, Uḥud is in the foreground and the mosque site about 4.8 km beyond; Qubāʾ lies further south still, on the side from which the Hijra party came.
reveal.basis: computed distances and bearings between gazetteer points

question.q: The song is sung everywhere at the Hijra. What do you expect its source to look like?

options.text: A late report with a broken chain, and its occasion debated
options.why: It rests on al-Bayhaqī's disconnected report, and Ibn al-Qayyim placed it at Tabūk.

options.text: A ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth in al-Bukhārī
options.why: Al-Bukhārī has the general joy of the people (al-Barāʾ), but not this song.

units.matters: Reflection: the joy of the welcome is firmly attested; the much-loved song that now carries that joy is a later, weaker witness. Both can be held honestly.

units.title: Emigrants and Helpers in the Qurʾān
units.kicker: How revelation named the two groups

statements.text: The Qurʾān describes the Anṣār as those who settled in the home and in faith before the emigrants, love those who emigrated to them, find no envy in their hearts for what the emigrants are given, and prefer others over themselves even when in need.
It names the first forerunners among the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār, and those who followed them in excellence, as those with whom God is pleased and who are pleased with Him.

Ibn Isḥāq says that by the time the houses were built, every household of the Anṣār had accepted Islam except Khaṭma, Wāqif, Wāʾil and Umayya, branches of the Aws known as Aws Allāh, who kept to their old religion for a time.
The name al-Anṣār, 'the Helpers', is the Qurʾān's own term, used alongside al-Muhājirūn in 9:100.

quran.gist: The poor emigrants, driven from homes and property, seek God's favour; and those already settled in the city and in faith love them, hold no grudge, and give them preference even in hardship.
quran.context: Read here as the Qurʾān's own portrait of the two groups whose bond this act follows. Established as text; its link to the brotherhood is thematic.

quran.gist: God is pleased with the earliest of the emigrants and helpers and those who followed them well, and has prepared gardens for them.
quran.context: The verse groups both communities together as forerunners. Established as text.

discover.label: Look over the oasis at dusk

reveal.text: The oasis sits in a basin with lava fields to east and west and Uḥud to the north: a small, enclosed space for two peoples to share.

question.q: 59:9 praises those who prefer others 'even when they themselves are in need'. Which episode in this act shows that most clearly to you?

options.text: Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ offering half his wealth
options.why: Reported in al-Bukhārī.

options.text: Abū Ayyūb and Umm Ayyūb mopping water with their only blanket
options.why: Reported by Abū Ayyūb in Ibn Isḥāq.

units.matters: Reflection: scripture gave the two groups lasting names and praised each for what it gave up or gave away.

units.title: Counting time from the Hijra

when.label: Under the caliph ʿUmar, about year 16 or 17

statements.text: Sahl b. Saʿd reports that the Companions did not count years from the Prophet's mission ﷺ nor from his death, but from his arrival in Madinah.
Al-Ṭabarī places the decision to date by the Hijra in the caliphate of ʿUmar, in the year 16 (some say 17).
statements.note: The reports differ between year 16 and 17.

statements.text: Reports also differ on why the year was made to begin in Muḥarram rather than in Rabīʿ al-Awwal, the month of arrival; one account has it as the month when pilgrims returned home.

sources.ref: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī, commentary on al-Bukhārī 3934

statements.note: Varying reports on who proposed Muḥarram and why.

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq's own dating already runs from the arrival: he says the Prophet ﷺ stayed in Madinah 'from Rabīʿ al-Awwal to Ṣafar of the following year' while his houses were built.

discover.label: From Makkah to Madinah, the line that became a calendar

reveal.text: The roughly 340 km between the two cities, in a straight line, is the journey the Islamic calendar counts from.

question.q: From which event did the Companions choose to count the years?

options.text: The Prophet's arrival in Madinah ﷺ
options.why: Sahl b. Saʿd says so explicitly.

options.text: The first revelation
options.why: Sahl says they did not count from the mission.

options.text: His death
options.why: Sahl says they did not count from his death either.

units.matters: Reflection: of all possible beginnings, the community dated itself from a move, not a birth, a battle or a death.

units.title: Whoever's hijra is to God

when.label: Sayings from the Madinan years; the end of hijra after the Conquest, year 8

statements.text: ʿUmar reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: actions are only by intentions, and each person has what he intended; whoever's hijra is to God and His Messenger, his hijra is to God and His Messenger, and whoever's hijra is for worldly gain or to marry a woman, his hijra is to what he emigrated for.
A later report says the ḥadīth was prompted by a man who emigrated to marry a woman called Umm Qays; Ibn Ḥajar notes that nothing in that report shows it was the occasion of the saying.

sources.ref: al-Ṭabarānī, al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr, from Ibn Masʿūd
Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī, on ḥadīth 1

statements.note: The 'emigrant of Umm Qays' story is attested, but its link as the occasion of the ḥadīth is not established.

statements.text: Ibn ʿAbbās reports the Prophet ﷺ saying on the day of the Conquest: 'No hijra after the Conquest, but jihad and intention; and when you are called to go out, go out.'

ʿĀʾisha explained that believers used to flee with their religion to God and His Messenger for fear of being tried, but once God had made Islam prevail, a person could worship his Lord wherever he wished.

Another report, 'hijra will not end until repentance ends', is graded differently by scholars, who reconcile the two by distinguishing the obligatory hijra from Makkah, which ended, from leaving sin or a land where faith cannot be practised, which does not.
statements.note: The chain of this report is criticised by some and accepted by others; the reconciliation is a scholarly interpretation.

reveal.text: Makkah, Thawr, the coastal stages, Qubāʾ, the valley of the first Friday and the mosque site: the stations of this journey seen at once.

discover.label: Return to where the camel knelt

reveal.text: The drying-ground of two orphans became the Prophet's mosque, which today stands on the site.

question.q: If the hijra from Makkah ended with the Conquest, what in the ḥadīth of intentions still applies to you?

options.text: Every move and every action is judged by its intention
options.why: The ḥadīth begins with intentions in general before giving hijra as its example.

options.text: 'Jihad and intention' remain after the Conquest
options.why: The words of Ibn ʿAbbās's report.

units.matters: Reflection, not fact: the Hijra was a journey of a few hundred kilometres, but the sources treat it as the founding of a community: a mosque, a brotherhood, a compact and a calendar. Its lasting lesson, in the Prophet's own words as transmitted, is that what counts is what one moves toward, and why.
